title: Nicholas Owen (22 March)
hookLine: a carpenter who built priest-holes in English houses and died under torture

cards: In some old English country houses, a guide will stop beside a fireplace, a staircase, or a stretch of plain wall, and press something. A panel swings open. Behind it is a space barely big enough to crouch in.
Visitors call them priest-holes, built for Catholic priests to hide in when searchers came to the door, and some of them, tradition says, were built by one small man with a carpenter's tools.
People called him Little John. His name was Nicholas Owen.

teach.b: In Nicholas Owen's England, it was a crime for a Catholic priest to say Mass, and a priest who was caught could be put to death for treason. Families who kept the old faith hid priests in their homes.
Nicholas became a Jesuit brother, not a priest, and he used his trade.
He worked, tradition says, mostly at night, alone, after receiving Communion, telling no one but the household.

He built hiding places so well that searchers could tear a house apart for days and find nothing: false floors, hollow walls, spaces behind chimneys, sometimes one hiding place built to be found so the real one stayed hidden.
Then he was caught. After days in hiding at a house called Hindlip, hungry and cramped, he came out, tradition says, partly to draw the searchers away from the priests still hidden.
He was taken to the Tower of London and tortured, hung by the wrists again and again, to make him name the houses and the priests.

teach.h: HANDS IN THE SERVICE OF OTHERS.
teach.b: He never did. He died there, and was canonized with other martyrs of England and Wales. It was a cruel age on more than one side, and the Church remembers him not for hating anyone, but for keeping people safe.

teach.h: IS NOT THIS THE CARPENTER'S SON?
teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims, the people of Jesus's home town ask: "Is not this the carpenter's son?" Nicholas Owen served God the way a carpenter can: with his hands, in silence, for other people's lives.

how: Catholics in England and Wales remember Saint Nicholas Owen with the other martyrs of England and Wales, and the Jesuits keep his memory; visitors to some old English houses can still see hiding places attributed to him.

o: a Jesuit carpenter who built priests' hiding places
an English priest who said Mass in secret
a Tower guard who helped prisoners escape

p: the house where he was caught
where he was tortured and died

s: Nicholas Owen was a Jesuit priest
he was a Jesuit brother, a carpenter, not a priest.
he sometimes built one hiding place meant to be found
tradition says a decoy kept the real hiding place safe.
under torture he named the houses he'd worked on

games.q: you've been hiding for days in a cramped space. priests are still hidden nearby, and the searchers won't leave. what do you do?
o: come out, and draw the searchers away.
try to slip past and escape.
games.why: tradition says Nicholas came out partly to draw the searchers away from the priests. he was taken to the Tower and never gave anyone up.

practice: Look at your hands and turn them over, and think of what they can do that someone near you needs: fix a hinge, cook a meal, carry a bag, sew a button, hold a hand.
If you pray, offer your hands to God for that work; if you don't, rest them open on your knees and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Nicholas Owen. A Jesuit brother and carpenter who built hiding places for priests in English houses, and died under torture rather than give anyone away.

orig.note: Greek: a builder or craftsman, the word for carpenter in Matthew 13:55.

carryVoice: Your line: the builder of hiding places. He kept others safe and never gave them away. That's day nine hundred seventy-six.
